title: Security deposits
text: At the start of a tenancy a landlord may not require more than: the first month's rent, the last month's rent, a security deposit equal to no more than one month's rent, and the cost of a new lock and key. A security deposit must be held in a separate, interest-bearing account in a Massachusetts bank, and the tenant must receive a receipt identifying the bank and account within 30 days. The landlord must pay the tenant 5 percent interest (or the actual interest earned) each year. Within 30 days of receiving the deposit or the start of the tenancy, the landlord must give the tenant a signed statement of the condition of the premises. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends the landlord must return the deposit with interest, less only lawful deductions for unpaid rent, an agreed increase in real estate taxes, or reasonable damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, supported by a sworn, itemized list of damages with documentation. A landlord who fails to return the deposit within 30 days, fails to provide the itemized list, holds the deposit in a commingled account, or uses a lease with a clause forfeiting the deposit, forfeits the deposit and is liable for three times the amount wrongfully withheld, plus 5 percent interest, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Waiver of statutory rights void
text: Any provision of a lease or other rental agreement by which a tenant waives, or purports to waive, rights and remedies provided by law is against public policy and void. A landlord may not require a tenant to agree to terms that strip statutory protections such as the warranty of habitability or security-deposit rights.

title: Quiet enjoyment; interference with utilities
text: A landlord who willfully or intentionally fails to furnish water, hot water, heat, light, power, or gas required by the tenancy, or who directly or indirectly interferes with the tenant's quiet enjoyment of the premises, or who attempts to regain possession other than through lawful court process (including by changing locks, removing belongings, or shutting off utilities), is liable to the tenant for actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, together with the costs of the action and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Reprisal for reporting violations or organizing
text: A landlord may not threaten, take, or serve a reprisal against a tenant for reporting housing-code violations to a public body, for pursuing or asserting legal rights, or for joining a tenants' organization. Conduct such as an eviction, a rent increase, or a substantial reduction in services within six months of the tenant's protected activity creates a rebuttable presumption of unlawful reprisal. A landlord who violates this section is liable for the tenant's actual damages or between one and three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Notice to quit for nonpayment of rent
text: A tenancy at will may be terminated for nonpayment of rent only after the landlord gives the tenant a written 14-day notice to quit. A tenant who has not received such a notice within the prior twelve months may cure and reinstate the tenancy by paying all rent due, together with interest and costs, on or before the answer date in any resulting eviction action.

title: Notice to terminate tenancy at will
text: A tenancy at will may be terminated without cause by either party by written notice. The notice period must equal the interval between rent days or 30 days, whichever is longer. A no-cause termination that provides less notice than the statute requires is defective.

title: Habitability defense and rent withholding in eviction
text: In a summary process (eviction) action for nonpayment of rent or for termination without fault, a tenant may raise, as a defense or counterclaim, that the landlord breached the implied warranty of habitability or violated a statute or code affecting health or safety, provided the landlord knew of the conditions before the rent was withheld and the conditions were not caused by the tenant. Rent may be withheld or abated to the extent of the diminished value of the premises, and the tenant may not be evicted for nonpayment of rent that was lawfully withheld once the tenant pays the amount found due by the court.

title: Repair and deduct
text: If a landlord fails to remedy a violation of the State Sanitary Code that may endanger health or safety within a reasonable time after receiving notice, and the violation was not caused by the tenant, the tenant may arrange for the repair and deduct the reasonable cost from future rent, up to four months' rent in any twelve-month period, without being liable for eviction on that basis.

title: Unfair or deceptive acts unlawful
text: Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are unlawful. In the residential rental context, conduct that violates landlord-tenant statutes or regulations — such as mishandling a security deposit, charging unlawful fees, or renting premises unfit for habitation — constitutes an unfair or deceptive practice.

title: Consumer remedies; multiple damages and attorney's fees
text: A person injured by an unfair or deceptive act may, after sending a written 30-day demand for relief, recover actual damages or $25, whichever is greater. If the act was a willful or knowing violation, or if the respondent refused a reasonable settlement offer in bad faith, the court may award double or treble damages and, in a successful action, reasonable attorney's fees and costs. This remedy is commonly available to tenants for landlord violations of the security-deposit and habitability statutes.
